issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: Military-themed conversations are hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 51-year-old school principal; this trigger implies a combat-related context not represented anywhere else in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar People: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar
issues.explanation: Avoiding people involved in the event or who look similar fits interpersonal/assault/accident traumas better than life-threatening illness, where there are typically no 'other people involved' in that sense. It is not well supported by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'talking about the future' as a trigger is plausible, but 'alcohol smell' is hard to connect unless alcohol was part of treatment context; nothing else in the profile supports that association, making this trigger set clinically incoherent.

'People can't be trusted' is more typical of interpersonal trauma and is poorly anchored to a life-threatening illness trauma in the absence of any treatment-related betrayal, conflict, or mistrust themes elsewhere in the profile.

'Crying' is not a trauma cue but an affective response/behavior, so it is clinically incoherent as a trigger item relative to the other trigger items, which are concrete sensory reminders linked to life-threatening illness (alcohol smell, hospital/antiseptic smell).

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: A global mistrust appraisal is a poor fit for the rest of the profile and trauma type. In life-threatening illness, the other items center on altered self and self-reliance, while 'People can't be trusted' implies an interpersonal betrayal/threat theme that is not supported by the memory, trigger, or strategy items and does not align well with the otherwise weak/inactive Threat links.

vignette: Thomas, a 51-year-old school principal, found himself grappling with a reality that felt increasingly unrecognizable. After a life-threatening illness last year, he was left with the haunting memories of his hospital stays, where the antiseptic smell still seemed to linger in the air around him. Those scents now triggered a visceral response - a tightening in his chest and a wave of anxiety that made him want to retreat into the safety of his home. He had begun to avoid any environment that reminded him of the hospital, cutting off contact with friends and family as a way to shield himself from the pain of those memories. As he isolated himself, each reminder of his trauma only deepened his conviction that he was fragile, leading him to adopt even more strategies to avoid situations where he might feel vulnerable or exposed. Every time he experienced a trigger, like the scent of antiseptic, he felt a strong urge to withdraw and avoid those situations altogether, reinforcing the maladaptive strategies he had started to rely on. With every encounter that reminded him of his hospital experience, he felt compelled to withdraw further; it was easier to avoid the discomfort than to confront the anxiety that arose from those memories. Each time he caught a whiff of alcohol, whether from a passing colleague or a bottle left unopened in his kitchen, it sent him spiraling into a state of distress that led him to isolate completely. Thomas often felt trapped in a loop of rehearsing conversations in his mind, agonizing over how to respond if he had to interact with anyone. The idea of a medical exam or procedure filled him with dread, a reminder of the vulnerability he had experienced during his illness. The anticipation of these interactions became a trigger, deepening his resolve to avoid medical cues altogether. Each time he encountered a reminder of his hospital experience, whether it was the scent of antiseptic or the sound of a medical device, he found himself retreating further into avoidance - convinced that he was too fragile to face the world. The intensity of these reminders made the memories of his hospital stays flood back, causing him to relive the panic he had felt at that time, which reinforced his desire to stay away from anything that might trigger those feelings again. As he recalled those overwhelming memories, the emotional weight of the past solidified his negative appraisals, causing him to believe even more strongly that he was incapable of coping with anything that reminded him of those experiences. He believed that if he could just steer clear of hospitals, ambulances, and even the faintest scent of antiseptic, he could keep the memories at bay. But every time he chose to avoid a reminder, it reinforced his belief that he was incapable of facing his trauma, leading him to feel even more fragile and reinforcing his negative self-appraisal. This belief that he was weak and vulnerable led him to feel threatened by even benign reminders, as he interpreted them as signals that he was in danger of experiencing the same trauma again. The memories of his hospital experiences only served to amplify his self-doubt, making him feel as though he was perpetually on the edge of another breakdown, thus increasing his sensitivity to triggers that might evoke those memories. Once he concluded that the world was filled with potential threats, even ordinary situations began to feel perilous, making him hyper-vigilant to reminders that could trigger his anxiety. This conviction that he was weak warped his perception of ordinary situations, where he began to view benign reminders as threats, reinforcing his anxiety and deepening his resolve to avoid them. Each time he avoided these triggers, he felt a fleeting sense of relief, but he soon found himself using this avoidance as a crutch, reinforcing the idea that he was too fragile to face the world. Yet, each time he tried to forget, the bodily reenactments emerged, causing him to feel as if he were reliving those moments of panic - his heart racing, palms sweating, as if he were lying in a hospital bed once more. Each act of avoidance just confirmed to him that he was unable to cope without it, further entrenching his belief that he was unworthy of support and reinforcing a sense of inadequacy. His struggle with memory was profound. Thomas found it difficult to deliberately recall the specifics of his illness; the effort only brought a flood of emotion without clear images or context, leaving him feeling vulnerable and exposed. He would sit for hours, lost in thought, unable to grasp the fluidity of his past while simultaneously feeling the weight of its emotional intensity. With each struggle to recall his experiences, he felt the memories come rushing back with an emotional weight that intensified his sense of inadequacy, making him believe he was permanently changed and unable to reconnect with who he once was. The more he struggled to recall the specifics of his illness, the more he felt the urge to escape into avoidance, believing that disengaging from the world was the only way to shield himself from the painful memories. Each time he was confronted with those memories, he found himself retreating further into avoidance, convinced that staying away from reminders would prevent the emotional turmoil from resurfacing. The fear of not being able to trust his own body loomed large in his mind, further complicating his attempts to engage with the world. This conviction that he could not rely on himself made it difficult for him to remember times when he had felt strong or capable, leading him to focus only on moments of perceived failure and reinforcing his negative self-view. This conviction that he was weak made him hyper-aware of any physical discomfort, turning every ache or twinge into a reminder of his vulnerability and triggering a rush of anxiety. Every time he felt unwell, a familiar panic would rise, confirming his belief that he could no longer rely on himself. The body that had once been a source of strength now felt like a traitor, reinforcing his negative self-appraisal. Every time he recalled the memories of feeling weak and unwell, he could not shake the feeling that he was permanently altered, which only solidified his negative beliefs about himself and his inability to cope with life's demands. Each instance of physical discomfort became a reminder of the frailty he perceived in himself, making the memories of his illness more vivid and reinforcing the idea that he was no longer the person he used to be. As Thomas's negative appraisals deepened, he found himself spiraling further into maladaptive strategies. The person he had become felt unrecognizable, a shadow of his former self, and the isolation became a coping mechanism. He could hardly endure the thought of explaining his situation to others, fearing their pity or misunderstanding. Each act of avoidance reinforced his belief that he was unworthy of support, creating a cycle where his loneliness confirmed his negative self-image and further distanced him from those who might offer help. With every time he chose to withdraw rather than reach out, he felt the weight of his belief that he was incapable of being understood or accepted grow heavier, further entrenching his negative self-view. This belief that he was unworthy of support made him withdraw even more, resulting in a self-fulfilling cycle of loneliness and despair. His interactions with others diminished, and he began to see triggers everywhere, from patients in the waiting room at his doctor's office to the faint smell of disinfectant in the school corridors. The more he engaged in avoidance behaviors, the more he realized how many situations had become triggers, reinforcing his belief that he was unable to participate in life without feeling overwhelmed. This avoidance not only deepened his isolation but also created a landscape of triggers that loomed larger in his mind, as he became increasingly aware of every situation he could no longer face. His belief that he was fundamentally fragile made him interpret everyday cues, like a colleague's cough or the sound of a siren, as immediate threats, leading him to engage in avoidance strategies that further isolated him from his surroundings. As he continued to avoid these interactions, the growing list of things he could no longer face became a constant reminder of his trauma, reinforcing his belief that he was unworthy of support and further isolating him from potential sources of comfort. With every encounter that reminded him of his trauma, he felt the world closing in, confirming his belief that he was unworthy of support and fueling his desire to retreat further into isolation. Each time he chose to engage in avoidance, he told himself it was necessary to protect his fragile state, but this only deepened his conviction that he was incapable of facing the world, further entrenching his negative self-image. Over time, the avoidance strategies he adopted led to a further entrenchment of his negative appraisals. He would sit alone in his home, ruminating on how profoundly different he felt, questioning whether he would ever regain a sense of normalcy. The memories of his illness haunted him, and each time he attempted to engage with the world, he felt a mixture of dread and disconnection. These haunting memories consistently reminded him of his perceived fragility, which made him lean more heavily on avoidance strategies to escape the pain, further entrenching his feelings of inadequacy. These haunting memories not only solidified his fears of inadequacy but also made him question whether he could ever truly be free from the shadow of his trauma, leading him to seek refuge in avoidance. These haunting memories served as a constant reminder of his perceived fragility, and he found himself increasingly relying on avoidance strategies to escape the pain, which only deepened his feelings of inadequacy. His thoughts spiraled, reinforcing the narrative that he could no longer trust himself or his body. This cycle of self-doubt and negative appraisals kept drawing him back to the painful memories, as he found himself constantly reliving moments that confirmed his perception of being broken. The once-vibrant principal who led his school with confidence now felt like a ghost, an unrecognizable figure struggling to reclaim his life. Seeking help felt like an insurmountable challenge, but after months of isolation, Thomas finally reached a breaking point. He realized that he could no longer bear the weight of his memories and fears alone. What he feared most was the possibility that he would remain trapped in this cycle forever, but the hope of reclaiming his identity, of reconnecting with his life and his loved ones, pushed him to seek professional support. In that moment of vulnerability, he recognized that seeking help might be the first step toward finding himself again. This overwhelming emotional response made it hard for him to confront the past, reinforcing the notion that he was permanently changed and unable to engage meaningfully with his life. This persistent avoidance only solidified his belief that he was fundamentally flawed, making him even more reluctant to confront the memories that haunted him, as he feared they would only confirm his worst fears about himself.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not convey how triggers lead to the use of maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not show how negative appraisals influence memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not indicate how negative appraisals impact the perception of triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not illustrate how memory influences the development of maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not demonstrate how maladaptive strategies reinforce negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not indicate how maladaptive strategies lead to increased perception of triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."

vignette_attempts.vignette:
Thomas, a 51-year-old school principal, found himself grappling with a reality that felt increasingly unrecognizable. After a life-threatening illness last year, he was left with the haunting memories of his hospital stays, where the antiseptic smell still seemed to linger in the air around him. Those scents now triggered a visceral response — a tightening in his chest and a wave of anxiety that made him want to retreat into the safety of his home. He had begun to avoid any environment that reminded him of the hospital, cutting off contact with friends and family as a way to shield himself from the pain of those memories. As he isolated himself, each reminder of his trauma only deepened his conviction that he was fragile, leading him to adopt even more strategies to avoid situations where he might feel vulnerable or exposed. Each time he caught a whiff of alcohol, whether from a passing colleague or a bottle left unopened in his kitchen, it sent him spiraling into a state of distress that led him to isolate completely.

Thomas often felt trapped in a loop of rehearsing conversations in his mind, agonizing over how to respond if he had to interact with anyone. The idea of a medical exam or procedure filled him with dread, a reminder of the vulnerability he had experienced during his illness. The anticipation of these interactions became a trigger, deepening his resolve to avoid medical cues altogether. Each time he encountered a reminder of his hospital experience, whether it was the scent of antiseptic or the sound of a medical device, he found himself retreating further into avoidance — convinced that he was too fragile to face the world. The intensity of these reminders made the memories of his hospital stays flood back, causing him to relive the panic he had felt at that time, which reinforced his desire to stay away from anything that might trigger those feelings again. He believed that if he could just steer clear of hospitals, ambulances, and even the faintest scent of antiseptic, he could keep the memories at bay. This belief that he was weak and vulnerable led him to feel threatened by even benign reminders, as he interpreted them as signals that he was in danger of experiencing the same trauma again. This conviction that he was weak warped his perception of ordinary situations, where he began to view benign reminders as threats, reinforcing his anxiety and deepening his resolve to avoid them. Each time he avoided these triggers, he felt a fleeting sense of relief, but he soon found himself using this avoidance as a crutch, reinforcing the idea that he was too fragile to face the world. Yet, each time he tried to forget, the bodily reenactments emerged, causing him to feel as if he were reliving those moments of panic — his heart racing, palms sweating, as if he were lying in a hospital bed once more. Each act of avoidance just confirmed to him that he was unable to cope without it, further entrenching his belief that he was unworthy of support and reinforcing a sense of inadequacy.

His struggle with memory was profound. Thomas found it difficult to deliberately recall the specifics of his illness; the effort only brought a flood of emotion without clear images or context, leaving him feeling vulnerable and exposed. He would sit for hours, lost in thought, unable to grasp the fluidity of his past while simultaneously feeling the weight of its emotional intensity. With each struggle to recall his experiences, he felt the memories come rushing back with an emotional weight that intensified his sense of inadequacy, making him believe he was permanently changed and unable to reconnect with who he once was. The more he struggled to recall the specifics of his illness, the more he felt the urge to escape into avoidance, believing that disengaging from the world was the only way to shield himself from the painful memories. The fear of not being able to trust his own body loomed large in his mind, further complicating his attempts to engage with the world. This conviction that he could not rely on himself made it difficult for him to remember times when he had felt strong or capable, leading him to focus only on moments of perceived failure and reinforcing his negative self-view. This conviction that he was weak made him hyper-aware of any physical discomfort, turning every ache or twinge into a reminder of his vulnerability and triggering a rush of anxiety. Every time he felt unwell, a familiar panic would rise, confirming his belief that he could no longer rely on himself. The body that had once been a source of strength now felt like a traitor, reinforcing his negative self-appraisal. Each instance of physical discomfort became a reminder of the frailty he perceived in himself, making the memories of his illness more vivid and reinforcing the idea that he was no longer the person he used to be.

As Thomas’s negative appraisals deepened, he found himself spiraling further into maladaptive strategies. The person he had become felt unrecognizable, a shadow of his former self, and the isolation became a coping mechanism. He could hardly endure the thought of explaining his situation to others, fearing their pity or misunderstanding. Each act of avoidance reinforced his belief that he was unworthy of support, creating a cycle where his loneliness confirmed his negative self-image and further distanced him from those who might offer help. With every time he chose to withdraw rather than reach out, he felt the weight of his belief that he was incapable of being understood or accepted grow heavier, further entrenching his negative self-view. This belief that he was unworthy of support made him withdraw even more, resulting in a self-fulfilling cycle of loneliness and despair. His interactions with others diminished, and he began to see triggers everywhere, from patients in the waiting room at his doctor’s office to the faint smell of disinfectant in the school corridors. As he continued to avoid these interactions, the growing list of things he could no longer face became a constant reminder of his trauma, reinforcing his belief that he was unworthy of support and further isolating him from potential sources of comfort. With every encounter that reminded him of his trauma, he felt the world closing in, confirming his belief that he was unworthy of support and fueling his desire to retreat further into isolation.

Over time, the avoidance strategies he adopted led to a further entrenchment of his negative appraisals. He would sit alone in his home, ruminating on how profoundly different he felt, questioning whether he would ever regain a sense of normalcy. The memories of his illness haunted him, and each time he attempted to engage with the world, he felt a mixture of dread and disconnection. These haunting memories not only solidified his fears of inadequacy but also made him question whether he could ever truly be free from the shadow of his trauma, leading him to seek refuge in avoidance. These haunting memories served as a constant reminder of his perceived fragility, and he found himself increasingly relying on avoidance strategies to escape the pain, which only deepened his feelings of inadequacy. His thoughts spiraled, reinforcing the narrative that he could no longer trust himself or his body. This cycle of self-doubt and negative appraisals kept drawing him back to the painful memories, as he found himself constantly reliving moments that confirmed his perception of being broken. The once-vibrant principal who led his school with confidence now felt like a ghost, an unrecognizable figure struggling to reclaim his life.

Seeking help felt like an insurmountable challenge, but after months of isolation, Thomas finally reached a breaking point. He realized that he could no longer bear the weight of his memories and fears alone. What he feared most was the possibility that he would remain trapped in this cycle forever, but the hope of reclaiming his identity, of reconnecting with his life and his loved ones, pushed him to seek professional support. In that moment of vulnerability, he recognized that seeking help might be the first step toward finding himself again. This overwhelming emotional response made it hard for him to confront the past, reinforcing the notion that he was permanently changed and unable to engage meaningfully with his life. But with each instance of avoiding social interactions, he could feel the weight of his self-doubt grow heavier, as if he was continuously reinforcing the idea that he could no longer trust himself to connect with others. This persistent avoidance only solidified his belief that he was fundamentally flawed, making him even more reluctant to confront the memories that haunted him, as he feared they would only confirm his worst fears about himself.
